She was the one who had organized the trip, who had spent a whole Saturday making sure everyone's visa paperwork was right, and she looked at the two shapes with the patience of a person who intended to understand. "Okay, so this one looks like an actual pyramid. Like, Egypt. And this one looks like an upside-down one, or a lightbulb."

Xavier held the Niger chart up. Wide at the bottom, narrow at the top, a triangle so clean it could have been drawn with a ruler. "So the bottom bars are the youngest ages," he said. "Zero to four, five to nine, all that. If the wide base is the young part, then that's a high birth rate and a young population." He set it down and picked up the other. "And this one's wide at the top. Old at the top means the young part is small." He stopped, hearing himself state it plainly for the first time. "So for Niger, the thing they'll run out of is classrooms. Schools and teachers. Japan's the opposite problem. It's going to need nursing homes."

Maria frowned at the pyramid in her hands. "You're sure the bars aren't, like, women on one side and men on the other?"

"They are, actually. Both sides together. But the shape's the point." He rotated the chart ninety degrees so the age groups stacked upward like floors of a building, youngest at the bottom, and Maria said, "Oh. It's a picture of the whole country standing on its children."

Behind them a television mounted from the ceiling ran a news segment about a populist senator who wanted to close the border, and a woman waiting nearby said to her companion, not quietly, that politicians had been trying to subjugate ordinary people since the beginning of time and this one was no different. Shaylee, who had gone to buy them all water, came back during this and distributed the bottles, saving the cold one for Xavier because he got headaches when he didn't drink enough, which she knew because she'd been on the robotics trip with him last spring.

"They're boarding us," Mr. Russo said, arriving at the bench with his lanyard swinging. The choleric businessman was gone, either pacified or rebooked onto someone else's flight. He glanced at the charts still spread across the bench and Xavier's finger resting on the wide base of the Niger pyramid. "Did you finish?"

"Mostly," Xavier said, and gathered the pages before Mr. Russo could read them. He wanted to arrive at the answer himself, or at least arrive at the part of it he could defend. "I think I know what the shape means. Wide base, young population, they're going to need more schools and teachers, way more than nursing homes. But I don't know how fast, or whether the town we're going to has any schools at all, or whether the government is already building them and we'd just be in the way."

Mr. Russo considered this for a moment, then began collecting the group's daypacks. "Then ask them when we land," he said. "The teachers, I mean. Ask what they actually need."

In the jetway, packed into the slow shuffle of boarding passengers, Maria leaned close. "The lightbulb country," she said. "Japan. What happens to it?"

"Nobody to take care of the top," Xavier said. "But that's fifty years out. It's a guess with good posture."

Shaylee snorted so loudly that the man in front of them turned around, and she apologized, still laughing, and the three of them moved forward with the line, Xavier holding the charts against his chest, the wide base of one country pressed to his heart.

activity: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
knowledge_domain: to predict how a change in temperature shifts a reaction at equilibrium using Le Chatelier's principle
fact: The principle is named after the French chemist Henry Louis Le Chatelier, who stated it in 1884.
story:
The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and vinegar, because somebody at the next table had built a volcano. Makayla set her display board on the folding table, propped the beaker of cobalt chloride solution in front of it, and plugged in the hot plate she had borrowed from Ms. Virtanen, who had made her sign a form promising to replace it if she desiccated the entire sample into a crust of blue crystals, which had happened once during practice.

Her board said "Shifting Equilibrium with Temperature." Below the title she had taped two photographs: the solution pink in a bowl of ice water, the same solution blue after sitting on the hot plate. That was the part she understood. When you heated it, it went blue; when you cooled it, it went pink; and when you left it alone, it sat somewhere in between, a muddy purple that looked like a bruise. The judges were supposed to come by at ten.

At nine fifteen, Titus arrived at the table next to hers with a model of a hydrogen fuel cell and a tri-fold board with laminated diagrams. "You put the ice in the beaker?" he said, looking at her setup.

"In the water bath. Around the beaker. There's a difference."

"I'm just saying, if the heat makes the reaction go faster, then it's just collision theory with extra steps."

Makayla had wondered about this for two days, and the honest answer was that she didn't think that was it, because the color went back. A faster reaction would just finish; it wouldn't march blue and then retreat to pink like something being pulled. But she couldn't say why the pulling happened, only that it did, and she suspected that "it does it because it does it" was not a winning sentence in front of judges. "It's not about speed," she said. "It's about balance."

"It's about you hoping nobody asks why," Titus said, and went to straighten his laminates.

The fair was held in the annex of the science museum, which the school rented because the gym's ceiling had a leak over the badminton courts, and at nine forty, while Makayla was coaxing the recalcitrant hot plate to warm up at all, Mohamad appeared beside her holding a museum brochure and a bag of vending machine pretzels. He had finished setting up his mold-growth experiment early, since mold required considerably less equipment than chemistry did. "There's a wall out there," he said. "Equilibrium stuff. Big panels. Nobody's looking at it because there's a dinosaur skeleton in the way."

"I can't leave my table."

"Judges are on the far side talking to the volcano kid. He's erupting for them right now. There's a line."

She went. The wall was in the chemistry corridor, past a case of amalgam samples, mercury mixed with other metals in little sealed tubes, and behind a banner about reactions that run forward and backward at once. One panel showed the same color change she had on her table, pink and blue, with a caption underneath. The principle is named after Henry Louis Le Chatelier, a French chemist who stated it in 1884. Makayla read it twice. There was a small portrait of a man with a beard who looked, she thought, like a substitute teacher about to confiscate something.

"The principle is named after Henry Louis Le Chatelier," Mohamad read aloud, chewing a pretzel. "French guy. 1884. So it's not just a rule, it's a guy's rule. That means you can say 'according to Le Chatelier' and sound like you read books."

"His name's on the wall and I've been calling it 'the balance thing' in my head for a week." She took a picture of the caption with her phone. The panel said the system responds when you change something about it, that a change in temperature shifts the balance one way or the other, and it did not say why, which Makayla found almost comforting, because the museum apparently didn't know either, or had decided not to say.

Back at the table, Ms. Virtanen was waiting with a clipboard and two other judges, one of whom was holding a cup of coffee and examining the ice bath as though it might be decorative. "So," Ms. Virtanen said. "Walk us through it."

Makayla lit the hot plate properly this time, and while the solution sat in its bath of ice, pink and steady, she told them what she had done twenty times at home: heat it, and it shifted blue; cool it, and it shifted pink; and it always came back, it never picked a side and stayed. She said that she used to think heat just made things go faster, and that she had been wrong, that this was a different idea, about a reaction balancing itself against whatever you did to it. She pointed at the photograph of the purple solution. "It's an equilibrium. The forward and backward reactions are both happening. When I change the temperature, the balance shifts, and Le Chatelier is the one who stated how it works, in 1884." The coffee judge wrote something down. The other one leaned in as the solution, now on the hot plate, began its slow turn from lilac to a clean and definite blue.

"Why does it shift that direction and not the other?" the coffee judge asked.

Makayla looked at the beaker. "I don't know yet," she said. "The panel at the museum doesn't say either. It's on my list."

Ms. Virtanen wrote something too, but shorter, and turned her clipboard face down against her hip, which Makayla had never seen her do.

After the judges moved on to Titus and his fuel cell, Mohamad slid a folded page onto her table, torn from the back of his mold notebook, with a note written in the amalgam of print and cursive he used when he was being sincere and pretending not to be. "You said 'I don't know' to a judge," it read. "Bold strategy. The mold is winning, by the way. Don't tell the judges it's winning." Makayla folded it again and put it in her pocket, then lifted the beaker off the hot plate with her tongs and set it back into the melting ice.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: The Haggadah is the book read aloud at a Passover Seder; it retells the story of the Israelites' exodus from slavery in Egypt.
story:
Grandma Ruth's dining room smelled of chicken soup and furniture polish, and the good tablecloth had already lost its first battle with a glass of Manischewitz, spilled by a cousin who would remain, at Jordan's insistence, nameless. "You're leading tonight," Grandma had announced in February, as if conferring a knighthood, and Jordan had spent the weeks since then reading the Haggadah on the bus, the way other kids crammed for chemistry. The Haggadah, he'd discovered, was the book read aloud at the whole Seder; it retold the story of the Israelites' exodus from slavery in Egypt, start to finish, and tonight every page of it was his responsibility.

The problem arrived before the soup did. His younger cousin Sadie, eight years old and drunk on the power of a new reading level, had pulled him into the hallway and demanded a speaking part. Then his uncle, who considered all ritual a form of unpaid theater, muttered that he'd "sit through it, but nobody's giving me a script." Meanwhile Bentley, who had come along because his own family's spring break involved a cabin with no wifi, stood in the doorway holding the extra Haggadah Grandma had dug out of the sideboard, wearing the expression of a boy who suspected he'd been handed homework on a vacation.

"You know I'm not Jewish, right," Bentley said, not quite a question.

"You know this book doesn't care," Jordan said. "It's basically a very long story about leaving Egypt, and everybody at the table is supposed to get a turn reading it out loud. That's the whole system." He said it lightly, but he meant it as a promise, and promises at this table had a way of being remembered until the next millennium.

He did the candle blessing with hands that only shook a little, and Grandma nodded once, which from her was applause with confetti. Then came the puzzle he'd actually been dreading: the reading itself. Fifteen people, one book per table cluster, and a tradition that wanted every voice included, from Sadie to the uncle to Bentley, who was technically a guest and technically now holding page twelve. Jordan's grandfather, before he died, had simply gone around the table in order, and Jordan had loved that, the democracy of it. But order meant the long Middle passages landed on the people least able to survive them, and Sadie would get a paragraph in a language she hadn't learned yet, and the uncle's sarcasm would curdle the Four Questions.

So he split the difference, which felt less like a decision and more like a confession that he had two opinions. Sadie got the short, punchy sections, the plagues, which she delivered like a weather report announcing hail with genuine relish. Bentley got the narrative parts, the actual story of leaving Egypt, because a newcomer deserved the plot and not the fine print. The uncle got nothing at first, and when the uncle raised an eyebrow, Jordan said, "You're on commentary. You're allowed to be sardonic about the matzah, it's tradition," and the uncle, caught off guard by being wanted, actually read his page straight through.

Between the brisket and the dessert, Grandma caught him in the kitchen rinsing a serving spoon. "Your grandfather went in order," she said, in the tone of someone opening a negotiation.

"I know. I contextualized it a little." He hadn't planned to use the word; it fell out of him, and he braced for teasing.

But Grandma only tilted her head. "Your grandfather had twenty years of practice before he started rearranging. You did it on your first try, and nobody complained."

"Uncle Jeff complained about the parsley."

"Uncle Jeff would complain about a tax refund." She handed him a dry towel. "You know your cousin Debbe called, she wants you to run it next year at her house in Boston. She says her Seder's been chaos since Zayda died."

Jordan dried the spoon and thought about that while the dryer hummed. He'd spent weeks trying to find the one right way, as if leading were a math problem with a clean answer, some kind of rationalism of the table where if you arranged the readers correctly the evening would prove itself. But the evening hadn't felt solved; it had felt steered, and only barely, and half his choices had been guesses he couldn't defend. Whether his system was better than his grandfather's, or just newer, he genuinely did not know, and he found he could hold that without it itching.

Back at the table, Sadie had appointed herself distributor of the afikomen hunt clues and was being extremely corrupt about it. Bentley leaned toward Jordan and said, quietly, "The exodus part was good. The part with all the rabbis arguing, I didn't follow a word."

"Nobody follows that part. That's the part where everybody gets more wine."

"Then I understand it perfectly."

Jordan picked up the Haggadah again, licked his thumb, and turned toward the closing hymns. "Okay, table," he said. "Last stretch. Sadie, you start us off, loud as you want."

Sadie stood up on her chair. Nobody stopped her.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A preprint is a paper posted publicly before peer review, so its findings have not yet been checked by independent experts chosen by a journal.
story:
The public library smelled of carpet cleaner and old glue, and Clara had claimed the corner table by the window an hour before anyone else thought to want it. Two articles lay in front of her, both about whether later school start times improved adolescent sleep, and both, at first glance, equally authoritative. She had found them through the same search, read the same abstract style, noted the same tidy scatter of statistics. Ms. Quinn had assigned each of them a critical review that compared the two pieces of scholarship, weighing their methods against each other and arriving at a considered judgment. Clara had assumed the hard part would be the writing. She was beginning to suspect the hard part was the deciding.

Tiago dropped into the chair across from her with a granola bar and no apology. "You're still on that thing? You've been on that thing since Tuesday."

"Both articles say the opposite thing," Clara said. "One finds big effects on grades, the other finds almost nothing. And I can't figure out why, because their methods look the same to me."

Tiago leaned over and turned a page with a granola-dusted thumb. "This one's weird. It doesn't have a journal name on it. Where'd you even get it?"

Clara looked down at the first article, the one with the confident tone and the dramatic findings, and saw that Tiago was right. Above the author list there was no journal, no volume number, only the name of a server and a string of letters and digits, like a license plate. Her second article had all the furniture of publication: a journal title, an issue, a DOI printed in small type like a serial number. She had transcribed both citations onto her notecard in identical format, and in doing so she had made them look like the same kind of thing. They were not.

She opened her laptop and typed the license-plate string into the search box. The article came up on a public server, posted by its authors, stamped with a date and a bright orange banner she had somehow scrolled past the first time. She read the banner twice. A preprint, it said, is a paper posted publicly before peer review, so its findings have not yet been checked by independent experts chosen by a journal. Below that, a line noting the version, and below that, a comments section where two strangers were arguing about the sample size.

"So?" Tiago said, watching her face change. "What's a preprint?"

"A paper posted online before anyone's checked it," Clara said. "Not peer reviewed. It just sits there." She said it flatly, the way you repeat a rule you've just been handed, and then the rule began to move through everything she'd written. The dramatic findings weren't published findings. Nobody chosen by a journal had gone through the numbers yet. The other article had been through that gauntlet, slow and dull as it was, and had emerged with smaller, hedged, almost moribund conclusions: modest gains in sleep duration, no clear effect on grades.

For a while neither of them said anything. The window had gone from bright to the flat gray of late afternoon, and somewhere behind the reference desk a printer was grinding through someone else's work. Clara thought about how easy it would be to treat the two articles as equals, to write that the evidence was "mixed," and let the reader shrug. There was a version of that move she'd used before, in English essays, calling it nuance when really it was surrender. Ms. Quinn had written something in the margin of her last paper that she'd been avoiding thinking about: "Two views disagreeing is not the same as both being right." At the time Clara had dismissed it as a teacher's tic. Now it looked more like a warning against a certain lazy relativism, the kind that dresses up indecision as open-mindedness.

But she didn't want the opposite failure either, dismissing the preprint as worthless just because it was early. The comment section argument, whatever else it was, was real people engaging with real numbers in public. Some preprints became important. Some collapsed. This one's findings had not yet been checked, which meant it wasn't wrong; it meant she didn't know yet, and a reviewer she'd never meet might know in six months. She pulled her notecard toward her, crossed out the citations, and rewrote them side by side with a line between them, then wrote at the top of a fresh page: "The published study is weaker in effect but stronger in standing. The preprint is stronger in effect but unverified." She underlined nothing. She sat with the sentence, chewing the cap of her pen.

Tiago gathered his wrapper and stood. "You're going to be here forever, aren't you."

"Probably," Clara said. She clicked back to the orange banner, opened the comments, and began to read.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: A food bank is usually a central warehouse that collects and distributes food to local agencies, while a food pantry is where people pick up food directly.
story:
Peyton arrived at the loading dock at eight sharp, the way the confirmation email had instructed, and stood beside a metal door propped open with a milk crate. Inside, shelves rose to the ceiling, stacked with canned corn and pasta in flats, and a man in a lanyard waved her toward a folding table where a sign-in sheet waited. She wrote her name, then her school, then the hours she hoped would look responsible on an application she hadn't finished.

"You're the new one," said Kierra, who had been at the table since seven and had already claimed the good stool. "Fair warning, the sorting is interminable. Last time I did rice for three hours." She held up her palms as evidence, dry and powdery. Peyton laughed, and the morning began with dented cans pulled from a pallet, each one to be adjudicated: swell it, tip it, label intact or not, keep or toss. Mr. Francis, the volunteer coordinator, moved between them without comment, trusting them to make the calls.

By ten, Peyton had expected the doors to open. She had imagined a line, a counter, groceries handed across it, the whole picture assembled from photographs on the organization's website. Instead the dock stayed quiet and a box truck idled at the bay, being loaded by two men with dollies. She counted the clock's second hand through one full rotation before she asked. "When do people come?"

Kierra looked up from her rice. "Nobody comes here. This is the food bank."

Peyton waited for more, and got none. "Then who's it for?"

"The pantries. It goes out to them." Kierra nodded at the truck. "Food bank's the warehouse that collects everything and distributes it to the local agencies. The pantries are where people actually pick up the food." She said it flatly, the way you recite something you were once confused about yourself, and went back to the rice.

So the picture Peyton had carried all morning, the one where she stood behind a counter and looked someone in the face, dissolved. She thought of her mother, months ago, at the kitchen table with the scholarship brochure, saying that service meant seeing people, not just logging hours. Peyton had agreed without argument, mostly to end the conversation, and had chosen this Saturday for the line on her application. It had seemed simple then: drive somewhere, hand over cans, feel the appropriate things. The warehouse offered no such transaction. She sorted a flat of beans and found she was sorting it faster than before, as if speed could settle the question of whether the work counted when no one was there to receive it in person.

Mr. Francis put a hand on the table beside her. "We're short on the pantry run," he said. "You want to ride along to St. Bridget's? They open at noon." She nodded before she'd finished deciding.

The truck took a route she half knew, past the pharmacy and the fields behind the middle school, and she sat in the cab with her hands folded on her backpack. Her father had driven her down this road once, years ago, the summer before sixth grade, when the factory where he'd worked cut its second shift. He had pointed out almost nothing, but she remembered now that he had known the turns by heart, and that they had come home with a box she wasn't allowed to look through, and that neither of them had mentioned it again. She had assumed, at eleven, that it was something for someone else. It had never once occurred to her to ask.

At St. Bridget's, the pantry turned out to be a church basement with folding tables and a line already formed, and the unloading was fast, heavy, and warm. Peyton carried flats to the far table, and when she straightened up, Alaina from her chemistry class was third in line, holding a numbered ticket, her little brother gripping the hem of her jacket. Alaina saw her. For a moment neither of them moved, and then Alaina lifted her chin slightly, a small declaration that she would decide what this was, and Peyton found she was glad of that, glad to be denied the easier role of the one who gives.

She went back for another flat. Kierra was stacking cans along the table's edge, and Peyton set her box down beside her and kept her eyes on the work. "Next Saturday," Kierra said. Peyton said, "Same time," and slid the last can into place.

activity: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
knowledge_domain: to debate whether an ancient religious rule still applies in modern life using the text itself
fact: Leviticus 19:9-10 commands farmers not to reap the corners of their fields but to leave them, and the fallen gleanings, for the poor and the stranger.
story:
Kai spread the printout across Lily's kitchen table and tapped the underlined verse with two fingers. "It's from Leviticus 19, verses 9 and 10. It commands farmers not to reap the corners of their fields but to leave them, and the fallen gleanings too, for the poor and the stranger." Lily copied it onto an index card, then looked up at the window above the sink, where her mother's tomato plants leaned against the glass, and said nothing.

The cultural festival was in four days, and their debate slot was titled "Does an Ancient Rule Still Apply?" Ms. Novák had assigned the format herself: argue only from the text, no appeals to authority, no statistics. She had said it once, in the hallway, and refused to say anything more. "Figure out what the words are actually asking," was all she'd offered, and then she'd walked off toward the gymnasium, keys jingling.

Blake arrived carrying a grocery bag of snacks and a counterargument he'd clearly rehearsed on the bus. "Nobody farms," he said, dropping into the third chair. "We live in apartments. The rule is about corners of fields and gleanings, fallen grain. It's agricultural. It doesn't apply."

"That's the easy version," Lily said, and was surprised at how sharp it came out, because Blake was the one who usually said things like that to her.

She remembered, suddenly, being eleven, at her grandmother's table, the summer before her grandmother stopped recognizing people. There had been a plum tree at the edge of the yard, and her grandmother had always left the last plums on the highest branches, windfall ones too, bruising on the grass. Lily had asked why she was wasting them. "Not wasting," her grandmother had said, pressing the knife flat against the cutting board. "Leaving." A boy from down the lane, the one whose father had lost his job at the plant, came with a paper bag every few days and took what had fallen. Nobody ever called it anything. It had seemed, at eleven, like a small eccentric habit. Now it sat in Lily's mind next to the index card like a key beside its lock.

"Okay," she said slowly, turning the card over. "Here's my problem with your position, Blake. You're saying the rule dies with the fields. But if the whole thing collapses when the farm disappears, then the rule was never about anything but farming, and I don't think that's what the words are doing." She read the card aloud again, and the phrase snagged her each time: the poor and the stranger. "It names the people, not just the crops. It builds the stranger in. Any stranger."

"So translate it," Kai said, pulling the bag of pretzels open. "What's a corner of a field now?"

Lily stood up and started pacing the narrow space between the table and the counter. "What we leave. Deliberately don't take. Not what we donate after we've reaped everything, not a check written at year end to subsume the whole question under organized charity. What we structurally leave behind. The margins. Maybe the rule says you're allowed to own a field, but the edges of it were never fully yours." Blake was frowning, but it was the frown he got when an argument was working on him rather than against him.

"That's a nice sentiment," he said. "Try cross-examining it. Someone will say: so should a grocery store leave shelves unreaped for the poor and the stranger? Should I leave my paycheck's corners?" He grinned, but Lily wrote it down, because it was a real hole.

She wrote for a while, and the kitchen went quiet except for the fridge and the pretzel bag. The honest version, she decided, was the one she couldn't fully close. On one side of the card she put her position: the rule's logic survives its original soil because it's about designed incompleteness, an ownership that stops short of the edges, and it binds whoever holds more than they need, field or no field. On the other side she wrote the questions she couldn't answer: how much leaving is enough, who counts as the stranger, whether a rule can be binding when nobody agrees what its corners are. She thought of telling the audience that she'd had a subpoena once, in her head, from her grandmother's plum tree, a summons she'd ignored for five years, and then decided that was too much, that some things you kept for yourself even while arguing in public. But she kept the image.

At the festival, in the folding-chair half of the gymnasium, the debate ran eighteen minutes. A student in the second row asked exactly what Lily had feared: whether the rule means anything for people who do not farm. Lily talked about margins, about margins of harvests and of paychecks, about leaving what falls. Blake, in the rebuttal slot, surprised her: he argued her side, not because she'd won but because, he said afterward, "you left the question open, and I kept trying to close it, and it wouldn't close." Ms. Novák scored the round, said "good instincts, unfinished thinking, which is better than the reverse," and moved on to the next pair of chairs. That evening Lily found her mother in the kitchen, cutting tomatoes from the window box, and asked if they could leave the last few on the stems this year. Her mother looked at her for a long moment, then at the tomatoes, and said, "Who are they for?" and Lily said, "I don't know yet."

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The coefficients in a balanced chemical equation give the ratio of moles that react, not the ratio of masses.
story:
The quiz came back on Tuesday with a red circle around Vincent's answer, and beside it Mr. Andersen had written only "see me," which was worse than a wrong mark would have been, because it meant the wrongness had a shape he was supposed to recognize. He sat through lunch with the paper flattened on the table, ignoring his sandwich, running his pencil down the problem again. Given so many grams of a reactant, find the grams of product. He had divided by the wrong thing, or multiplied by the wrong thing, and the answer he'd gotten was absurd, ten times too large, the kind of number that would mean a thimble of powder producing a bucket of salt.

"Move over," Annabel said, dropping her tray beside his. She leaned over the paper without asking, the way she habitually did with anything he was working on, as if his desk space were partly hers by long custom. "Oh, that one. I got it wrong too. Everyone got it wrong."

"Jaylynn didn't," Vincent said. Across the cafeteria Jaylynn was demonstrating something with her hands, wide gestures, retelling some triumph, and Vincent already knew from third period that her quiz had come back without a single mark on it.

"She says she just followed the equation." Annabel stole his apple out of pure reflex. "The numbers in front, the coefficients. Whatever they are."

"The coefficients," Vincent repeated. He said the word slowly, tasting it, because he had skipped the word every time he read the chapter, sliding past it the way he slid past words that looked like furniture. He wrote the balanced equation out again at the bottom of the quiz, the little numbers sitting in front of each formula like small polite doormen, and then he wrote Jaylynn's method underneath it, which was the same as his own method, and looked at both until his eyes ached. Whatever he had done, he had treated those numbers as if they applied directly to the grams, to the masses, and Jaylynn plainly had not. The an old adage his grandfather used, measure twice, cut once, drifted through his head, and he thought that the problem was not that he had measured once but that he had used the wrong ruler entirely.

He found Jaylynn in the chemistry room after last period, where she was habituating herself to the lab benches before Friday's practical, standing at a balance with her sleeves pushed up, weighing out white powder onto folded paper with a patience that surprised him. He had expected her to be disaffected, one of those students who did the work with a shrug, but she wasn't; she was careful, almost solemn about it.

"Can I ask what you did on number four," he said. "The mole one."

"You divide by the molar mass first," she said, not looking up from the balance. "The coefficients in a balanced equation give the ratio of moles that react, not the ratio of masses. So you have to get into moles before the equation means anything." She tapped the paper with one finger, once, and Vincent stood there while the whole problem quietly turned itself inside out in his head. The grams were just the costume the moles arrived in. You converted, then the little numbers worked, then you converted back. His answer had been absurd because he had asked the doormen to carry pounds instead of people.

"Show me," he said, and pulled a stool up beside her, and for twenty minutes they worked problems back and forth, she watching the balance between them, he scribbling, both of them arguing mildly about rounding. He still didn't understand why the universe had chosen moles as its currency, or why the coefficients couldn't be trusted with anything else, and he said so, and Jaylynn said, "It just is," which he accepted the way you accept that water freezes at a certain point on the thermometer, without needing the thermometer explained.

Annabel watched the two of them from the doorway for a while before she came in, her apple core still in her hand. She set it down next to Vincent's notebook, looked over his shoulder at the fresh column of numbers, and said, "Okay, so I was multiplying the grams by the coefficients."

"Everyone was multiplying the grams by the coefficients," Vincent said, and handed her a pencil.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Around 1420 in Florence, Filippo Brunelleschi demonstrated linear perspective, the technique of drawing lines that meet at a vanishing point to show depth on a flat surface.
story:
Connor's grandfather kept a drafting table in the back room of the house on Melrose Avenue, and this was where Connor sat on the first week of July, drawing the hallway of that same house for a portfolio he had to mail in September. The art school wanted observation drawings, real spaces, and the hallway was the most real space he knew: the dark runner, the umbrella stand, the door at the far end with its brass knob worn to a shine. He had drawn it three times that morning, and all three times it had come out flat as a receipt.

"It looks like a diagram," said Cecilia, who had biked over with two popsicles and was now leaning on the table's edge, dripping orange onto the newsprint. "It looks like the plan of a hallway, not the hallway."

"It's all right there," Connor said. "The runner, the wainscoting, the light from the kitchen. I measured the door frames with a tape measure. Why does it look like nothing?"

She peered closer, as if the answer might be hiding between his pencil lines. "The far door is the same size as the near one. In a real hallway, wouldn't the far one look smaller?"

He told her that was the fault of the tape measure, that the door was the same width at both ends, and she said, "But your eye doesn't care what the tape measure says," and went to find the grandfather, who was in the garden arguing with his insurance agent on the phone about whether the policy would indemnify him for the pear tree the storm had split. That word had been in the air all week. Connor heard it through the window now, the old man insisting that a fallen tree was exactly what a man paid premiums for.

When the call ended, his grandfather came inside, washed his hands, and looked at the drawing for a long time without touching it. "You know what's wrong with it," he said. "You drew it with your surveyor's mind. Your somatic mind knows better. Your body walks down that hallway every day and feels it getting longer."

"That's a weird way to put it," Connor said, though he knew what he meant. His grandfather had been made to do some kind of body-awareness program after his hip surgery, and now he talked like that, as though the mind were a genus with several species in it, most of which nobody had classified.

Cecilia said, "There's a name for the trick he needs, I know there is, we did it in Ms. Haile's class with the streets." She took a fresh sheet and a ruler, and drew a road, then fanned the curb lines upward and inward until they crossed at a point she marked with a small x. "Vanishing point," she said. "Ms. Haile made us say it ten times."

"Nobody taught me that," Connor said slowly, but something was moving in him now, a curiosity he could feel in his sternum. He pinned a new sheet to the board and began again, this time marking the far end of the hallway with a dot just left of the kitchen doorway. He ruled lines from the corners of the near doorframe to that dot and let them run, and watched the walls tilt inward, the runner narrow, the ceiling drop toward the floor the way it actually did when you stood at the mouth of the hall and looked in. The brass knob at the far end, when he drew it small and half the size of the near hinges, sat in the paper like a real thing, a small sun at the end of a tunnel.

His grandfather, watching from the doorway with his hands folded, said, "Brunelleschi," and when they looked up, he shrugged. "Around 1420, in Florence, he showed this to the whole city. Filippo Brunelleschi. Lines going to a vanishing point, depth on a flat panel, like a window opening onto a street. People crossed themselves when they saw it." He tapped the drawing with one finger. "Five hundred years later a boy in my back room finds it with a ruler on a Tuesday, for a school application."

Later, after Cecilia had gone home and the afternoon had gone bronze through the window, Connor sat with the finished drawing and his older flat one side by side, and could not decide which one told the truth. The flat drawing had the measurements right; the perspective drawing had the experience right, and he kept turning between the two like a man with two maps of the same country. Ms. Haile had told them once that the eye was not a camera, but he had not believed her until tonight. He took out a letter he was drafting to the school, wrote "I have been learning about how looking works," and then sat looking at the sentence for a long time, pencil hovering, before he folded both drawings together and put them in the folder.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At Lunar New Year, many Chinese families give money in red envelopes to children and unmarried younger relatives, because red is associated with good fortune and warding off evil.
story:
The drive to Grandma's took an hour and Kate spent most of it arguing with herself about a red envelope. Her cousin Lydia, in the back seat, kept tapping her phone against the window and saying nothing useful at all. At the last stoplight before the old neighborhood, Kate finally asked her outright: do you think we're still getting hongbao this year? Lydia shrugged, which meant she had been wondering the same thing and had also decided not to be the one to say it.

The house smelled like star anise and fried dough the moment the door opened. Aunts called out greetings, the grandmother pressed oranges into their hands, and the table was already disappearing under dishes. Kate helped carry bowls from the kitchen, and every time she passed the coat rack she noticed the small stack of red envelopes on the hall table, thin, crisp, waiting like a question nobody had asked out loud. She was eighteen now. Adults were not supposed to want things, she felt, and yet wanting this small thing had followed her the whole drive.

Her grandmother's neighbor, Ms. Mercer, arrived after lunch with a plate of shortbread and stayed, as she did every year, because she had lived beside the family for two decades and liked the noise. She sat beside Kate while the aunts played cards and asked, quietly, what the red envelopes were for. Before Kate could admit she only half knew, Lydia leaned across the table. "Money," Lydia said. "Red is good fortune, it wards off evil. Kids and unmarried younger relatives get them."

Kate looked at the stack in the hallway and did the arithmetic she'd been avoiding. A child, yes. A younger relative, maybe. But unmarried, Lydia had said, and Kate was that, and eighteen was still young, though college would come in the fall and after college a job and after that, presumably, the settled, ossified shape of an adult life, the kind that gave envelopes rather than received them. The thought had a strange weight. It was not about the money, which was never much. It was about being on one side of a line she could not see.

The problem surfaced at the card table. One of the aunts, shuffling, said in a too-casual voice that maybe this year they should only give to the little ones, since Kate and Lydia were practically grown. Another aunt disagreed. The grandmother said nothing at all, which was how she said the most. Lydia went rigid beside Kate, and Kate realized her cousin had been counting on that money for a train ticket she hadn't told anyone about. Lydia had mentioned it once in November, offhand, a concert in the city with Martha, and then never again, which was how Lydia handled wanting things she couldn't afford.

Kate could have stayed quiet. Instead she turned to Ms. Mercer, who was watching the whole exchange with open curiosity, and found herself explaining what she was only just working out: that the tradition reached toward people starting out, that red meant luck and protection, that maybe the point was never an age but a season of life. She heard herself building the argument and wondered whether she believed it or only wanted to. Both, she decided. The distinction did not hold up under the grandmother's steady gaze anyway.

Later, while the little cousins chased each other around the kitchen, the grandmother went to the hallway and came back with two envelopes. She gave one to Lydia first, then held Kate's a moment before handing it over. "Next year you study," she said. "Luck is for the road." Kate took it with both hands, the way she had been taught as a child, and felt the paper's dry warmth, the stiffness of new money inside.

On the porch that evening, Lydia peeled hers open, counted, and let out a breath. Ms. Mercer had gone home; the aunts were arguing over the last of the cards; somewhere inside the grandmother was wrapping leftovers in newspaper for everyone to take. Kate did not open her envelope. She slipped it into her coat pocket, unopened, and wondered how long she could keep it that way, a small red argument against the idea that wanting things was something you had to outgrow.

"You're not going to look?" Lydia asked, leaning on the rail.

Kate pressed her hand flat over the pocket. "When I get there," she said. "First day. In the line at the coffee place."

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: In 1896, Swedish scientist Svante Arrhenius made the first calculation of how much Earth would warm if the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubled.
story:
The graph was printed on the back of a worksheet, and Amelia had been staring at it for eleven minutes when Alexe texted to say she was coming over whether or not Amelia answered.

"Answer what?" Amelia typed, but the doorbell went before she could send it. Alexe came in holding a laptop, a bag of sour candies, and the particular expression of someone who has done nothing and would like this to become someone else's problem. The presentation was tomorrow, third period, Mr. Flores had moved it up a week because the assembly schedule had eaten Friday. Their slides said things like "greenhouse effect: important??" with two question marks, which even Alexe admitted was not promising.

"You do the science part," Alexe said, dropping onto the kitchen floor beside the coffee table. "I'll do the design. Design is basically science."

Amelia looked back at the worksheet. The graph showed a line that climbed and climbed, decade after decade, with little seasonal teeth along the way like a saw. She understood the teeth, mostly. What she could not yet explain to herself, let alone a classroom, was the mechanism, how a gas that let sunlight through could then refuse to let heat back out. It sounded like a door that only locked from the inside. She said none of this. She said, "The line goes up."

"Profound," said Alexe.

Amelia's mother was in and out, reheating soup, and at one point she paused behind them long enough to say that when she was Amelia's age, nobody had put this on a test, which seemed to Amelia less an observation than an act of self-defense. On the counter, the radio murmured about a treaty conference collapsing, some delegation walking out, the usual sectarian grievance flaring up again over who should cut what first. Amelia found herself half-listening. If a whole polity could not agree on the problem, it was mildly comforting that her only obligation was to explain it to twenty-six seventeen-year-olds by nine in the morning.

She worked it out with a saucepan. Not literally, though she considered it. She wrote: sunlight in, infrared out, carbon dioxide absorbs the outgoing kind and sends some of it back down, which destabilizes the whole balance, the planet takes in more than it gives off, and the graph is the receipt. Then she crossed out "the receipt" because it sounded like something a TED talk would say. Alexe, over her shoulder, said "keep the receipt," and Amelia kept the receipt.

Then Alexe said, "Wait, but how old is this? Like, did nobody know until computers?" She was typing it into her phone already, mostly to avoid making slides. "Because my uncle says it's all new modeling, which means it could be wrong."

Amelia watched the search results load. It was not new. In 1896, a Swedish scientist named Svante Arrhenius had made the first calculation of how much Earth would warm if the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere doubled. Hand calculations. Pencil, presumably, and a very long winter in Stockholm. Amelia read it twice, then said it aloud so Alexe would stop scrolling.

"That's over a hundred years before satellites," Alexe said. "That's so much worse."

"It's not worse or better. It's just the first calculation," Amelia said, and then, because it mattered, "the first estimate of warming from doubling CO2." Though she was honest with herself about what stayed uncertain: whether the man thought warming was a good thing for Sweden, whether the numbers then were near the numbers now, whether first meant correct. The phone did not say. The phone mostly wanted to sell them a documentary.

Valeria texted at ten to ask if they had finished, then admitted she had finished hers on Sunday, then admitted that was a lie and she had done the title slide. Her want, as far as Amelia could tell, was to be the person who had done the title slide while other people suffered. Amelia sent her a photo of the graph with the line going up, and Valeria sent back a single flame emoji, which Mr. Flores would not have accepted as a citation.

They built the deck until midnight. Alexe did do the design, which turned out to mean making the Arrhenius slide look like an old Wanted poster, and Amelia let it stand because it was either that or argue. At the end her mother called goodnight from the stairs, the radio had gone quiet, and the graph still sat there on the table with its climbing line and its little seasonal teeth, patient as a bill.

"Okay," Alexe said, closing the laptop, "tomorrow you talk, I click the slides, Valeria takes questions she can't answer."

"Valeria takes no questions," said Amelia, and turned off the lamp.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: With typical use, about 7 in 100 people relying on the combined birth control pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy, often because doses are missed.
story:
The waiting room of the dental clinic had two chairs left empty when Cohen arrived, and Milla had taken the one beside the window, where the late sun came through the blinds and turned everything a faint, jaundiced yellow. She had the pamphlets spread on her lap like cards she was about to play. Cohen sat down with his folder of notes and did not open it.

"You're not going to do it from the folder tomorrow," Milla said. "They're freshmen. They watch your face, not your paper."

"I know how it works," Cohen said. "You say the pill is basically always fine and everyone relaxes."

Milla handed him a clinic pamphlet she'd taken from the rack by the reception desk, the one about contraception, and folded his hand around it. "Read the small part. Out loud."

He read it, and then read it again to himself. With typical use, about 7 in 100 people relying on the combined birth control pill for a year have an unintended pregnancy, often because doses are missed. He had told the practice group yesterday, in the basement of the student health building, that the pill was close to perfect if you took it. He had said it confidently, with the folder open, and nobody had corrected him because nobody knew.

"Seven in a hundred," he said. "Because of missed doses."

"That's why the nurse kept going on about setting a daily phone reminder," Milla said. "You asked me afterward if she was being fussy. She wasn't being fussy."

The receptionist called his name before he could answer. Mr. Somsak's office smelled of latex and something minty and chemical, and the chair reclined with a hydraulic sigh. Cohen had a wisdom tooth coming in sideways, an ache he'd ignored through exam week, and Mr. Somsak leaned over him with the little mirror and said, "You'll feel pressure, not pain. If it's pain, raise your left hand and we stop. You understand the difference?"

"I raise my hand and you stop," Cohen said, and Mr. Somsak nodded and gave him a form to sign first, a consent form, and Cohen read it all the way through, even with the clock running, even with the print small. There was a paragraph about indemnity, about not holding the clinic liable for outcomes that had been explained in advance. He signed it because it had been explained, because he'd been given the chance to say no, because the raised hand was his the whole time.

Afterward, with gauze packed against his gum and his words coming out thick around it, he sat back in the waiting room and worked. He could not speak the practice lines well with the cotton in, so he transcribed them instead, printing each sentence in the notebook while Milla watched and checked the pamphlet against what he wrote. Consent: you say what's going to happen, they can stop it at any time, a hand raised stops everything, the hand stays theirs even after the paperwork. Contraception: he wrote the number where he couldn't avoid it, seven out of a hundred in a year with typical use, missed doses, and next to it he wrote "say the reminder part, don't skip it." Testing: the campus clinic did it on Mondays, walk-in, results in a week, nobody's parents were called. He crossed out "basically always fine" and, after a minute, crossed it out a second time, harder, so it couldn't be read underneath.

"You're going to talk like that?" Milla said, nodding at his mouth. "Tomorrow, with a swollen jaw?"

"I'll talk fine by tomorrow. It's today I sound like this."

"That's not what I meant." She looked out the window at the parking lot, at the long light going orange on the hoods of the cars. She was leaving for a city six hours away in eleven days, a transfer she'd decided on in March and told him about in April, and both of them had been careful ever since, polite in a way they hadn't been before. "I meant you're going to stand up there and tell a hundred strangers things you got wrong two days ago."

"That's why I'm fixing them."

"You can't fix everything. Some kid's going to ask you something and you won't know, and you'll have to say you don't know." She said it without sharpness, the way she used to tell him his collar was crooked. "Can you do that? Say you don't know, in front of everyone?"

He thought about the nurse at the health building, how she'd said "that's a good question, ask the doctor, I don't want to guess" without seeming to shrink. He had admired it and hadn't understood until now that it was something a person decided to do, not something a person was. He wrote at the bottom of the page, "if I don't know, I say so," and left it there, uncertain whether the sentence would hold when the room was full.

The pamphlet still had a page he hadn't read, a diagram of how to use a condom that he'd have to explain without laughing and without letting the room laugh at somebody who didn't know. Milla picked up the notebook, read his lines back to him in a flat, nurse-like voice, and made him raise his left hand to stop her twice, until the gesture felt like something his arm knew.

At the door, with the gauze still in and the sun almost gone from the lot, she handed back the notebook and kept the pamphlet, folding it into her back pocket. "I'll read the rest tonight," she said. "Call me if your mouth hurts." Then she pushed through the glass door into the blue evening, and Cohen stood a moment with his hand raised, halfway between a wave and something else, before he put it down and dialed the clinic's number to ask whether Monday testing needed an appointment, the phone warm against his jaw.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: A 1985 study by Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky called basketball's 'hot hand' an illusion, but a 2018 reanalysis by Miller and Sanjurjo found a statistical flaw and evidence of streak shooting.
story:
Natalie had the good seat, the corner of the couch where she could see both the television and the front door, and she was not giving it up. Amber arrived at halftime with a bag of chips and her older brother's opinions, which she distributed like handbills. Ciara was already on the floor with her laptop open, pretending to do homework. In the kitchen, Natalie's father was shouting at the referee with a specificity that suggested he believed the man could hear him.

The player everyone had come to watch was a guard named Delacroix, who had scored eleven straight points in the third quarter. Amber pointed at the screen with a chip. "He's on fire. You have to feed him the ball every possession now. That's just basketball."

"That's not just basketball," Natalie said. "There was a study. Nineteen eighty-five. Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky. They called the hot hand an illusion." She had read about it three weeks ago, late at night, following a link from a forum argument about coin flips, and she had bookmarked it the way you bookmark something you expect to need in a fight you haven't had yet.

Amber rolled her eyes at Ciara, who kept typing. The living room had gone loud; Mr. Henry, the neighbor whose apartment shared a wall and who had been invited out of pity and building policy, leaned forward in the armchair with a saturnine expression, as though the whole evening were a verdict he'd already reached. Delacroix missed a jumper. Amber turned around slowly, arms spread, saying nothing, which was somehow worse than saying something.

But then Delacroix hit two more, and a three from the corner with a hand in his face, and the room erupted, and Amber shouted, "ILLUSION," over the noise. Natalie felt something in her recalibrate. It was one thing to hold a fact at midnight in a browser tab. It was another to hold it in a living room where everyone she knew was watching the same streak and seeing a man burning.

Ciara turned her laptop around. "There's a reanalysis," she said. "Miller and Sanjurjo. Twenty eighteen." Natalie took the computer. The paper argued that the original study had contained a statistical flaw, and that when it was corrected there was evidence of streak shooting after all. Natalie read the sentence twice. Amber, who had been mid-gloat, went quiet.

"So it's real," Amber said.

"It's evidence of it," Natalie said. "That's not the same as him having it right now." She could feel the two ideas in her hands like weights on opposite pans. The streak in front of her was one game, one night, a sample so small it could be anything. And still the correction mattered; the scientists had been wrong in a direction, and being wrong in a direction meant the folklore had survived on something more than luck. She did not know which of those things to trust while the fourth quarter counted down. She decided that not knowing was allowed, as long as she said so out loud.

"Then bet," Amber said. "If you believe in evidence of streak shooting, bet on Delacroix. If you believe in the illusion, bet on the team."

Natalie considered the stakes, which were the last of the chips and who had to carry Mr. Henry's folding chair back down the hall. She took the bet on the evidence, and Ciara wrote the terms in her notebook with the solemnity of a court reporter taking a deposition, naming the parties, the terms, and the time. Mr. Henry watched all of it without comment, his chin on his fist.

Delacroix took the last shot, a twenty-five footer with four seconds left, and missed the rim entirely. The ball went out of bounds off his own team. Amber collected the chips immediately, opening the bag over her face like a trophy. Natalie was still holding the laptop, still looking at the sentence about streak shooting, when Mr. Henry finally spoke from the armchair.

"Twenty years I watched this team," he said. "Delacroix's father missed that same shot, this same building, in ninety-one."

Ciara stopped writing. Amber lowered the chips.

"Run it back," said Mr. Henry. "Same angle, same leg. I'd know it in the dark."

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: With typical use, about 13 in 100 people relying only on male condoms for a year have an unintended pregnancy, mostly because condoms are not used correctly every time.
story:
The waiting room smelled of mint and something colder underneath it, and Dylan had his flashcards face down on his knee like a hand of cards he was ashamed to be holding. Ryan sat beside him with a magazine he wasn't reading, turning the same page every thirty seconds.

"You're doing it here," Ryan said. "Seriously. You're rehearsing a sex talk in a dentist's office."

"Tomorrow I stand up in front of thirty sophomores and I'm the one who's supposed to know things. So yes, here, now, please." Dylan squared the cards. "You be them. Ask me what they'd ask."

Ryan set the magazine down. "Fine. Condoms. Are they good or not?"

"They're good. They're the only method that protects against infections, and you can get them free at the clinic on Marsh Street, no appointment. But." Dylan paused, because this was the part he'd gotten wrong himself two weeks ago, in Ms. Horváth's classroom, when he'd said condoms were basically foolproof and she'd written a number on the board and waited. "With typical use, about thirteen in a hundred people relying only on male condoms for a year have an unintended pregnancy."

Ryan frowned. "Thirteen out of a hundred. That's terrible. The box makes it sound like ninety-something percent."

"The box isn't lying, exactly. But typical use means real people, real years, and mostly it happens because they're not used correctly every time. That's the part I have to get across without making them panic or making them think it's pointless."

"You're going to say a sentence with 'typical use' in it to fifteen-year-olds and expect them to hear anything after it."

Dylan laughed before he could stop himself, and a woman across the room lowered her newspaper an inch. "That's my whole problem," he said, quieter. "I keep building the speech like it's a debate, like if I get the numbers in the right order they'll just agree. And the numbers aren't even the hard part."

The receptionist called a name that wasn't his, and a man in a paint-spattered jacket went past them toward the back. Ryan watched him go, then said, "So what's the hard part."

"Consent. How do you explain it so it isn't a platitude? Everyone's heard 'no means no' so many times it just bounces off. I want to say it's ongoing, that you check, that being quiet isn't a yes, but when I write it down it sounds like a poster in a hallway." Dylan turned one card over, though he already knew what it said. "And the testing part. I have to tell them how to actually walk into a clinic and ask, which means telling them it's confidential, that you don't need a parent, that it's fifteen minutes and mostly just awkward."

"You've done it?"

"Last month." He hadn't planned to say that. He'd barely said it to himself, the Tuesday morning he'd taken the bus to Marsh Street with his student card and a lie about a dentist appointment, which was, he now realized, sitting in an actual dentist's waiting room. "I stood outside for ten minutes first. That's the part nobody tells you. The standing outside."

Ryan was quiet for a moment, and Dylan understood that this was new information between them, and that Ryan was deciding what to do with it. "Okay," Ryan said. "Then say that. Tell them about the standing outside. Skip the poster stuff."

"That's tangential, though. There's a curriculum, there's a checklist I'm supposed to cover."

"Is it? You said the hard part is getting them to hear it. They'll hear ten minutes of standing outside a clinic door. They won't hear a checklist."

Dylan looked at the cards in his hand, at the tidy numbered points Lily-Rose had helped him outline on her bedroom floor, highlighters and granola bars, and he thought about how certain it had all seemed laid out in neon yellow. He had wanted the presentation to be clean, defensible, nothing in it that could be argued with. But the arguable, imperfect parts were the true ones. The number on the board that had embarrassed him. The door he hadn't wanted to walk through. "I'd have to throw out half of this," he said, and heard that he was already doing it, already rewriting the opening in his head, and he hadn't even noticed his mind changing, which was maybe how it always happened.

"Dylan?" The hygienist stood in the doorway with a clipboard, and behind her, in the corridor, he glimpsed Ms. Horváth in the chair by the window, jaw stretched open, eyes closed, looking strangely like a student herself.

"That's my teacher," Dylan said, gathering the cards.

"Small town," Ryan said. "Go on. I'll be here when you come out, and I want to hear the version with the door in it."

Dylan stood, and in the mirror by the reception desk he caught himself grinning like someone who had already been given good news. He followed the hygienist back, and the last thing he heard was Ryan saying, "Thirteen out of a hundred, no, wait, don't tell me again, I'll look it up."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The FAFSA is the form US students complete to apply for federal financial aid such as Pell Grants and federal loans, and many states and colleges also use it to award their own aid.
story:
The mailbox was a green tin box on a crooked post at the end of the driveway, and by late afternoon Madison had opened it eleven times, which was ten more times than the mailman had come. Mr. Vargas, raking leaves across the street, had begun counting her trips out loud. "Twelve," he announced when she came down the driveway in her socks. "You're invigorating the whole postal service, kid. One girl, checking a box, and the federal government of mail is suddenly alert."

"It's not the mailman's fault," Madison said. "It's the college's fault. They said decisions would be mailed by Friday, and it is Friday, and therefore." She waved a hand at the empty box as though the logic was self-evident, which it was, to her. The letter inside, when it came, would either begin "Congratulations" or "We regret," and she had prepared herself for both outcomes by preparing herself for neither, which Elsa called a peccadillo but which Madison preferred to think of as strategy.

Elsa biked over after her own futile mailbox vigil, skidding to a stop in the gravel. "Mine's not here either. Nixon says his came yesterday and he's too scared to open it, so he's carrying it around sealed like it's a hostage." She dropped onto the driveway and lay flat on the warm concrete. "Do you ever think about how weird it is that a whole future fits in one envelope? Four years of your life, weighing less than a quesadilla."

Madison sat down beside her, less gracefully. She had been thinking about something else all day, something that had kept her and her mother at the kitchen computer until almost midnight, hunched over the FAFSA with the state aid deadline looming like a tide. The FAFSA was the form you filled out to apply for federal financial aid, Pell Grants and federal loans, and her mother had repeated the words like a prayer: Pell Grants, federal loans, federal aid. What Madison had not understood, until she'd clicked through the site herself while her mother hunted for a W-2 in a shoebox, was that it wasn't only the federal government that cared. Many states used it to award their own aid, and so did many colleges. One form, three doors. "So if we miss tonight," she had said, and her mother had said, "we don't miss tonight," and typed her Social Security number wrong twice, which was the peccadillo in question, though Madison would never say so.

"We filed at eleven fifty-eight," Madison told Elsa now, lying back on the driveway too. "Two minutes to spare. My mom made me read every field out loud like we were landing a plane. 'Dependent student.' 'Household size.' I dreamt about dropdown menus."

"You dreamt about dropdowns and you're the calm one." Elsa rolled onto her side. "Nixon would have passed out. Nixon passed out in line at the vaccine clinic. That's his whole personality."

The mail truck turned onto the street at four forty, driven by a man who took his diurnal duties with monastic serenity, delivering each house's pile as though the neighborhood were not a minefield of teenagers pretending to water plants they had never once watered before. When he reached the green tin box, he left one envelope, a thick one, thick as a sandwich, thick with the unmistakable density of good news plus housing brochures.

Madison carried it up the driveway without opening it, which Mr. Vargas found hilarious. "Twelve trips to the mailbox," he called, "and now you walk slow." She carried it inside, set it on the counter, and stared at it while her mother came in from the other room drying her hands. "Open it," her mother said, and then, softer, "No, wait. Do you want tea first?" Madison tore the end off the envelope like a bandage.

Congratulations, the first line said, and then financial aid, and then a sentence that made her mother laugh so suddenly that she had to sit down: the college could not determine her award until the FAFSA it had requested had been received and processed, which, given the two minutes to spare, might take a little time. They had raced a deadline for a college that had now, in its official letterhead voice, raced them right back. "So the answer is yes," her mother said, holding the page, "pending the answer to the answer." Madison picked up her phone to text Elsa, and typed, "Got in. Open yours, coward," and pressed send.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: In US college admissions, a college's yield is the percentage of students it admits who then accept the offer and enroll.
story:
The envelope from Hartwell College had been sitting on Avery's desk for nine days, unopened, because it was thin, and everyone knew a thin envelope meant no. She had carried it to school instead, folded into the back pocket of her binder, and now she was sitting in Mr. Gallagher's office during third period with the thing on her knee like a small animal she was afraid to wake.

"You can open it here," Mr. Gallagher said. He had a way of offering without pushing, hands flat on the desk, a mug of tea gone cold beside the file with her name on it. "Or you can put it in the drawer and open it in June. I have students do both."

Avery turned the envelope over. The flap had a Hartwell crest, gold foil, slightly crooked. "Ann says the thin ones are rejections. Kevin says that's a myth, that they email first anyway." She paused. "Kevin pontificates about admissions like he's been on a committee. He read an entire book about it in one weekend and now nobody can ask a simple question without getting a lecture."

Kevin was, in fact, the reason she knew anything at all about how colleges behaved behind their brochures. On the campus tour last fall, when the guide had boasted that Hartwell's yield was something to be proud of, it was Kevin who raised his hand and asked what that meant, and the guide, a senior in a green polo, had said, "Yield is the percentage of students we admit who accept the offer and enroll." Avery had written it on the margin of her tour packet. Later, waiting for the shuttle, she had thought about it longer than she meant to. A college was not just choosing her. It was also gambling on how many of its choices would say yes back.

That thought had changed which schools she'd listed on the form in front of Mr. Gallagher now. She had started out applying only to the two famous ones, the ones her mother called "the reach and the backup," which Avery privately considered a dysphemism for the backup, since calling it that made it sound like a punishment rather than a place. After the tour, she had added Hartwell, a school she actually liked, with a studio program and a river through campus, a school that admitted people it had some reason to expect would come. She understood, in a vague way she couldn't fully defend, that wanting her and expecting her were different things, and that she had spent a year applying to places that wanted students like her without expecting her at all.

"This is tangential," she said suddenly, "but can I ask you something that isn't about the envelope?"

"You can ask me anything that's legal."

"When I toured Hartwell, the guide seemed glad people came. Not glad like a salesperson. Glad like a host." She was watching her own hands. "And the other two places, the tour felt like they were letting us look at them. I keep thinking I should want the second kind. Everyone does. My mom does. And I changed my mind somewhere in October and I never told anyone."

Mr. Gallagher pulled a tissue box two inches closer to her side of the desk, a small adjustment he made without comment, and she took one even though she wasn't crying yet. "Did you list that on the form?" he asked. "The part where it asks why Hartwell?"

"I wrote three drafts. The last one was two sentences. 'The studio has windows on two sides. The guide knew the name of the woman who sweeps the gym.'"

She opened the envelope then, finally, with her thumbnail, because holding it closed had begun to cost more than knowing. The letter inside was one page, and the first line said the admissions committee was pleased, and she read it twice, and the second time she laughed, a short wet sound, and Mr. Gallagher said, "There's the backup," and she said, "Don't call it that. It's not the backup if it's the one I wanted."

Here was the part she hadn't expected, and she sat with it for a moment in the small warm office with the radiator ticking. The famous schools hadn't answered yet, and some part of her still wanted them to want her, still wanted the long envelopes and the phone calls and the story she could tell at graduation. That wanting hadn't gone anywhere. It was just that it now had to share the room with another one, and she did not know yet which would be louder by May, or what she would do if both spoke at once.

She folded the letter along its crease and put it back in the crooked envelope. "Can I put it in the drawer anyway?" she asked. "Just till the end of the day. I want to walk to sixth period knowing it's in here and not tell anyone till I decide what it means."

Mr. Gallagher opened the drawer, laid it flat between a box of transcripts and someone else's unclaimed schedule, and slid it shut. "It'll keep," he said, and handed her a pass for her next class.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Dry air at sea-level pressure breaks down and sparks at roughly 3 million volts per metre, which limits how strong a field can be across an air gap.
story:
Rebecca had taped the graph paper to the folding table by ten in the morning, and by eleven the gymnasium smelled of hot glue and floor wax, and her parallel plates, two squares of copper flashing screwed to a wooden frame, still hadn't produced a visible deflection on the foil leaf. She adjusted the separation to four centimetres with a ruler, wrote the number on the board beside her tri-fold, and watched the leaf hang straight down.

Her project was a field calculator. The idea was simple enough to fit on the display: enter the voltage across the plates and the distance between them, and the program returned the electric field strength at any point in the gap. She had tested it against the textbook examples, three of them, and it matched to two decimal places. What she wanted was a live demonstration, a small electroscope between the plates showing the field was really there, not just arithmetic on a screen.

Loick arrived from the chemistry row holding a cup of punch and looking at her board with his head tilted. "You're running twelve thousand volts," he said. "Across four centimetres. What does your program say the field is?"

She typed it in. The screen printed three hundred thousand volts per metre.

"Fine," Loick said. "But you wrote here you want to try the school's variable supply up to fifty thousand. Fifty thousand over four centimetres is a million and a quarter volts per metre. Is that a lot?"

"It's a big number," Rebecca said, and she meant it as a dismissal, but he kept standing there, drinking his punch, waiting in that way he had, patient to the point of being annoying. She looked at the number again. She had never asked what the ceiling was. Numbers on a screen didn't spark or burn; they just sat there.

Quintin wandered over from the robotics table in time to hear the last exchange. "Air breaks down," he said. "Dry air at sea-level pressure sparks at roughly three million volts per metre. That's the limit for a field across an air gap. Past that, you don't get a stronger field, you get a spark."

Rebecca wrote the figure on the corner of the graph paper and did the division twice. Three million volts per metre times her four-hundredths of a metre gap gave a hundred and twenty thousand volts, far beyond anything the school supply could produce. Her demonstration, even at its most ambitious, would sit comfortably below the ceiling. She felt something loosen in her shoulders, and then tighten again for a different reason, because she had spent three weeks treating the field as a pure output, a number with no world attached to it, and the world had a limit she'd never thought to look up.

Ms. Patel came by during the second judging block, read the board top to bottom, and asked what happened if the plates were moved closer together. Rebecca said the field strength would rise at the same voltage, and Quintin, who had stayed to watch the demo, said that if she got the gap small enough the same three million volt per metre figure would be crossed and the air would spark, even at modest voltages. Ms. Patel nodded once and moved on to the next table without comment, which was how she signalled that a student had answered well.

Rebecca pulled the plates in to half a centimetre and ran the numbers: twelve thousand volts over half a centimetre was two point four million volts per metre. Close. She nudged the separation down to three millimetres and the program printed four million. Over the limit, if the theory held. She connected the supply, told Quintin to stand back, and turned the dial slowly. At around nine thousand volts the gap gave a flat blue snap, a sound like a knuckle cracking, and the smell of something briefly burnt hung over the table. The judge at the far end of the row looked up.

The program had been right, and the world had confirmed it, and the two of them, the arithmetic and the spark, were now the same thing in her mind instead of separate rooms she visited one at a time. She wrote "demonstrated: 9 kV, 3 mm gap" under the printed prediction, then sat back on her heels. There were things she still couldn't account for. The humidity in the gym, the sharp edges of the flashing, the fact that the snap had come a little before the dial read the exact value her division predicted. She didn't write any of that down, but she didn't cross it out either.

Loick leaned over the table. "So your project failed?"

"No," Rebecca said. "It sparked." She picked up the ruler again and slid the plates apart, one centimetre at a time, watching the number on the screen fall back below the line where the air stopped obeying her.

activity: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
knowledge_domain: to analyse a population pyramid to predict whether a country will need more schools or nursing homes
fact: A pyramid whose base is narrower than its middle shows falling birth rates and an aging population, pointing to rising demand for nursing homes and elder care.
story:
The geography packet had been riding in the footwell of the car since Tuesday, and by Friday it had migrated under the seat, where it collected sunflower shells and one of Lina's hair ties. Elliot dug it out at a gas station outside Peterborough while his father paid and Chelsea claimed the good bench by the window.
