Mr. Ross, who was technically the neighbour and technically the driver and technically responsible for all three of them on this trip to his mother's eighty-eighth birthday, came back carrying four drinks and a bag of licorice that he defended as a Canadian birthright.

"Test on Monday?" Lina asked, peeking at the packet.

"Population pyramids." Elliot fanned the pages. "Two bars for every age group, men on one side, women on the other, and apparently the shape tells you the future, which sounds like astrology with spreadsheets."

"It's not astrology," Chelsea said, "because astrology doesn't have an axis."

Mr. Ross snorted into his coffee, and the car filled up again, and the packet stayed open on Elliot's knees all the way to the highway, mostly so he could pretend he wasn't carsick from reading.

The assignment was simple enough to be suspicious. Each student got a country and had to decide, from the pyramid alone, whether that country should be building more schools or more nursing homes in the next twenty years. Elliot had drawn Japan. Lina had drawn Niger. Chelsea, who claimed the universe punished her specifically, had drawn Canada, which she said was like being assigned homework about your own household.

"Niger is literally a pyramid," Lina said, holding up her page in the back seat. "Wide at the bottom, skinny at the top. A Christmas tree. Build all the schools."

"Japan's a weird one." Elliot turned his sheet sideways, then upside down, which improved nothing. "It's narrow at the bottom. Wide in the middle. It's like a spinning top. Or a wasp."

"It's an urn," said Mr. Ross from the driver's seat. "I've been to Japan."

At the party on Saturday, in a church hall that smelled like lemon disinfectant and coconut cake, Elliot ended up at a folding table with his grandfather's older sister, Great-Aunt Fay, who was ninety-one and had opinions about everything including his haircut. He told her about the assignment to have something to say. She ate her cake with terrifying efficiency.

"So you look at a picture," she said, "and you say whether my country needs more of me or more of you."

"Basically."

"And what did your picture say?"

"That the bottom of it is skinnier than the middle," Elliot said. "Fewer young people than middle-aged ones. Birth rates falling, population aging." He traced the shape in the air with two hands, tapering it inward at the bottom, widening it at his shoulders. "So, more nursing homes than schools. That's the answer the pyramid gives."

Great-Aunt Fay put down her fork. "Then who's going to work in them?"

The question sat there while a cousin refilled the tea. Elliot had a whole paragraph in his draft about elder care demand rising, and he suddenly could not remember writing a single line about who would staff it, as if buildings could care for people on their own. He looked down the hall at the rows of white and grey heads, at his own father carrying a chair for someone, at the one teenage boy on crutches eating a second slice of cake by the door.

"That's the part the pyramid doesn't show," he said slowly. "It shows who'll be there. Not who'll be holding the cups."

Back in the car on Sunday, he worked on the draft while Chelsea navigated and Mr. Ross recalibrated his route around a closed exit with the calm of a man who had been lost before and expected to be lost again. Elliot wrote the standard answer, the one the shape of the diagram demanded, and then, underneath it, he wrote the second part, the question Fay had left him holding, and he found he could not make the two fit together neatly. The diagram was like a rule, and the rule was true, and it still left the most important thing out.

"You look like a philosopher," Lina said. "Or someone doing math wrong."

"Both, probably." He read her his conclusion: the pyramid pointed toward nursing homes, but the real answer might be something the pyramid couldn't say, and he was going to hand that in even if it cost him marks.

"Bold," said Chelsea. "Mr. Ross, would you mark that down?"

"I once wrote an essay about my history teacher being an autocrat," Mr. Ross said, "and he failed me and also resigned, so I consider it a complicated win."

Lina laughed so hard she dropped the atlas, and Elliot folded his draft into his pocket, unfinished on purpose, and watched the fields go by, the licorice bag passing hand to hand in the falling light.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: Larger samples give more precise estimates, so a result from a small study carries a wider margin of error than the same result from a large one.
story:
Mia spread the two articles across the corner table of the cafe, pinning the curling edges with her mug and a jar of sugar, because Ms. Moose's assignment was due Thursday and she had promised herself she would start it Saturday, not Sunday, and here it was Sunday. Both articles asked the same question, whether a certain gene variant was linked to adolescent anxiety, and both reported that it was, roughly, sort of. She had read each one twice on the bus and could not have said, out loud, what she actually thought. The assignment wanted a critical review, a considered position, and all she had so far was a page of notes that said "both find effect???" three times.

Charlize slid into the other chair with an iced drink that sweated rings onto the table. "You look like someone stole your birthday."

"They agree," Mia said. "Both studies find the same association. So what is there to compare? I'm supposed to critique them, and they're just agreeing with each other."

"Nobody makes you compare two things that agree unless there's a trap." Charlize stole a sugar packet and folded it into a tiny triangle. "Read me the methods part. The boring middle bit. That's always where the trap lives."

Mia found the first article's methods section, the smaller study, the one whose authors wrote confidently about implications for screening. "They surveyed thirty adolescents. Selected from one school." She hesitated, because the number had snagged something in her memory, a half-remembered lecture from her stats unit that she had mostly slept through. She flipped to the second article. "This one surveyed thirty thousand. Across twelve countries."

Charlize leaned over, straw between her teeth. "So one's thirty and one's thirty thousand, and they both got the same answer?"

"Similar answers. Similar direction." Mia tapped the margin of the big study, where she'd underlined the confidence interval without understanding it. Then she found the same table in the small study, and the intervals were wide, wide enough that she could drive her whole argument through them. The memory assembled itself: larger samples give more precise estimates. A result from a small study carries a wider margin of error than the same result from a large one. So the thirty-person study hadn't exactly found what it claimed to have found; it had found something loose, something roomy. The thirty-thousand study had found the same effect in a much tighter grip. "Oh," she said. "Oh, that's the review. That's the whole review."

"Tell me in English."

Mia pulled her notebook over. "The small study's result could be way off, because the margin of error is wider when the sample is small. The big study's estimate is more precise. Same finding, different weight." She was already writing, an embryonic outline that she could feel structuring itself as the pen moved, thesis at the top like a flag planted in soft ground. "I can say both perspectives converge, but one deserves more trust than the other, and the paper that matters is the one that doesn't claim too much."

Charlize pointed her straw at the small article's conclusion, where the authors recommended genetic screening for anxious teens. "These guys found a wobbly number and built a whole policy on it."

"Which is the other half of my review." Mia felt something settle that she couldn't quite name, the difference between having read things and having a position. The small study had a virtue the big one lacked, though: it described its participants in detail, their environments, their families, even how the gene's observable effects, the phenotype, the anxiety itself, was measured hour by hour rather than once on a questionnaire. The big study saw far but thinly; the small one saw narrowly but deeply. That didn't augur well for a simple verdict, and maybe a simple verdict was the wrong thing to want. Maybe the honest review said: here is where they agree, here is why one estimate is more precise, and here is what no one can yet say, which was whether the variant mattered more in some environments than others. Both studies left that open.

"I still don't get why you're excited about homework," Charlize said, crumpling her napkin.

"Because I had two readings and no opinion, and now I have one." Mia capped her pen and squared the pages. "Ask me again Tuesday, though. I might read something tonight that changes it."

"That's not how opinions work."

"That's exactly how opinions work." She gathered the articles, small study on top, big study beneath, and slid both into her bag. At the counter she bought a second coffee, for the road, and Ms. Moose's Thursday suddenly looked like something she could meet standing up.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: The CDC advises against washing raw chicken, because the splashing water can spread bacteria to the sink and nearby surfaces.
story:
Eella turned on the tap and held the split chicken under it, the way her grandmother had done every Sunday of her childhood, water drumming against the skin and carrying a pink film toward the drain. She had the kitchen at the community center to herself until five, when the Friday meal service began, and she needed the braised chicken in the oven by four or the sauce would not have time to reduce. Her family was coming at six: her mother, her little brother, her grandmother herself, arriving by bus from the apartment with the good bread and the expectations.

Teegan, who had signed up for the same shift to finish a service requirement and stayed because he liked the knives, reached past her and shut the tap off with two fingers.

"What," Ella said.

"Teegan said don't wash it," Ayah offered from the counter, where she was peeling garlic with more force than the cloves required. She had her phone propped against the flour canister, a recipe on the screen. "He said it last week too, when the church group did that chicken."

"Because the CDC advises against it," Teegan said. He was already drying his hands. "Rinsing raw chicken splashes water around the sink and the counters, and it spreads bacteria onto everything nearby."

Ella looked at the bird in her hands, half rinsed, and then at the steel basin, which was dotted with fine droplets as far as the cutting board on her left. "My grandmother washed it her whole life. Nobody got sick."

"People get sick all the time," Ayah said. "They just blame the flu."

"That's not an argument." Ella set the chicken on the towel-lined sheet pan. She could feel the disagreement arranging itself into two positions, and she did not like either of them as stated. Her grandmother's practice was not superstition; it came from a place and a time when poultry was butchered in open markets and grit was a real problem. But Teegan's phone was showing her a page from the CDC now, held out flat across the sink, and the wording was plain. She read it twice. The splashing water carried bacteria to the sink and to nearby surfaces; that was the whole of it. Not a rumor, not a scare. An advisory with an etiology behind it she could look up later, a chain of causes she could almost see in the droplets drying on the steel.

"Fine," she said. "I'll pat it dry with paper towels and salt it. The browning works better that way anyway." She tore off towels and wiped down the basin and the counter and the board, methodically, and dropped the towels in the trash rather than the laundry basket where the cloth towels went. Ayah watched her do it and did the same with the garlic board without being asked.

They browned the chicken in the wide pan, skin side down, while Ella sliced onions until her eyes streamed, and Ayah deglazed with the cider Mr. Johansson had donated from his orchard along with a crate of apples nobody had time to peel. The sauce began to coagulate around the edges where it cooled, going glossy and slow, and Ella stirred it back in. Teegan took over the rice. At a quarter to five her grandmother arrived early, as she always did, and stood at the door of the kitchen with the good bread under her arm.

"You didn't wash it," her grandmother said. It was not a question. She had crossed the room and looked into the pan before Ella could decide whether to lie.

"No," Ella said. "The CDC says not to. The water splashes bacteria onto the sink and the counters around it." She kept her voice even, the way she would cite a source in a paper. "I patted it dry instead."

Her grandmother was quiet long enough that Ayah stopped chopping. Then she pulled a paper towel from the roll, tore it, and dried the rim of the pan where the sauce had spat, folding the towel into a neat square before throwing it away.

"In the market in Cairo, you washed it because you could see the dust," her grandmother said. "Here there is plastic on it. The rules are different when the chicken is different." She set the bread on the counter and looked at Ella. "You learned this from a screen."

"Teegan showed me," Ella said. She wasn't sure, suddenly, whether the difference between learning it from a screen and learning it at a grandmother's elbow mattered or whether it only seemed like it should. The advisory was the advisory either way. She thought of telling her grandmother that, and didn't.

At five the volunteers began arriving, and the meal went out at six, and her family took the corner table by the window. Her brother ate three pieces of chicken and her grandmother ate one, slowly, tasting it. When Ella came to clear the plates, her grandmother pressed the tines of her fork lightly against the emptied dish.

"Next time, less cider," she said. "And you will show me this page about the chicken."

Eella said she would, and gathered up the plates, and carried them back through the steam to the sink, where the water was already running for the wash.

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: A zero derivative does not guarantee a maximum or minimum: f(x) = x cubed has derivative zero at x = 0, but its graph keeps rising through that point.
story:
The smell of grandmother's house was cardamom and floor wax, and Mya had spread her calculus notes across the dining table as if declaring war on it. The exam was Monday morning. It was currently Sunday, four o'clock, and the light through the lace curtains had that late-afternoon quality of a deadline leaning on your shoulder.

"So," her grandmother said, setting down a plate of biscotti like a hostage offering. "You understand it now, or you are still copying?"

"I'm not copying." Mya angled her notebook away. "I'm deriving. It's different."

The problem was straightforward, which was exactly what made her suspicious. Find the derivative of f of x equals x cubed minus some mess of lower powers, set it equal to zero, solve, declare the maximum, collect the marks, go home. She had done four of these at the kitchen table last night, and Ms. Singh had written "See me" at the top of the page, which was teacher for something between a threat and an invitation.

Her phone buzzed against the wood. Rafael: did you figure out what singh wanted. Then Sukhman, in the group chat a minute later: she wrote see me on mine too. Mya typed back a thumbs up, which committed her to nothing, and pulled the notebook closer.

She worked through it. The derivative came out clean, three x squared and friends, and when she set it equal to zero everything collapsed down to x equals zero. Beautiful. A single critical point. She wrote "maximum" beside it with a flourish she would deny later, and drew a little roof over the word, a small grandiose peak, like a mountain in a child's drawing.

Her grandmother leaned over her shoulder, reading glasses low on her nose. She had spent thirty years at a utility company doing load calculations before anyone thought to call it engineering, and she had opinions about confident young people. "Graph it," she said.

"It's a maximum. I found where the derivative is zero."

"Graph it," her grandmother said again, and went to refill her tea, leaving the instruction behind her like a dropped gauntlet.

Mya graphed it, to prove her point, plotting x cubed minus nothing much, the simplest version of the family. She plotted minus two, minus one, zero, one, two. The points went up on the left, up on the right, up through the middle where they were supposed to crown themselves. She sat back. The curve rose through x equals zero like a guest walking straight through a party without stopping. The derivative there was zero, she had computed it herself twice, and yet the graph kept rising through that point, no peak, no valley, no roof. "It's not a maximum," she said to the kitchen. "It's nothing. It's just flat for a second."

Her grandmother returned with her tea and looked at the page. "A flat place is not a summit. A road can be level at the bottom of a valley or on a hillside or halfway up a climb. You checked your arithmetic. Now check your assumption."

Which was, Mya had to admit, a more elegant way of saying what Ms. Singh had probably wanted to say before deciding that writing two words and letting a student marinate was more efficient. She texted Rafael: zero derivative doesn't mean maximum. you have to graph it first. x cubed rises right through zero. Then she added, because honesty was cheaper before the exam than after: I got it wrong four times last night.

Rafael's reply was a string of exclamation points. Sukhman sent a photograph of her own notebook, four little rooftops marching across the page, each labeled maximum in increasingly confident handwriting. The group chat went quiet in the specific way it did when two people were frantically erasing.

Mya redid all four problems. She graphed each function before she wrote a word, and it turned out that some of her flat points were summits after all, and some were valleys, and one, the x cubed one, was just the graph pausing to catch its breath on its way up. The same derivative test, transmuted by one look at the actual curve, from a verdict into a clue. She thought about how she'd wanted the method to be a machine, something with the clean modularity of a vending machine, coin in, maximum out, no further attention required, and how it was actually more like a conversation where the function got a say.

At seven her grandmother brought soup, and Mya ate it one-handed while rechecking the second derivative on the last problem, which turned out to be the honest kind of zero, a real peak. The lace curtains had gone from gold to grey to black. She photographed her corrected pages and sent them to the chat, then packed her bag, zipper loud in the quiet room.

Her grandmother collected the biscotti plate, on which nothing had been eaten. "Tomorrow," she said, "when you are sure of something, draw the picture anyway."

"See me," Mya said, and pointed at the top of her notebook, at Ms. Singh's note, and laughed into her scarf as she pulled it on.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: On Mexico's Day of the Dead, orange marigolds called cempasúchil decorate altars and graves, because their bright color and strong scent are thought to guide the souls of the dead home.
story:
Daniel found the list on the fridge on Thursday morning, held there by a magnet shaped like a lime: call the florist, confirm the casserole dishes, marigolds. His mother's handwriting had gone small and careful since his grandmother died on Sunday, as if the letters themselves were trying not to disturb anyone. The funeral was Saturday. Today his mother wanted flowers for the altar they were building on the sideboard, because his grandmother had asked for that, in her way, near the end, when she stopped speaking English and spoke only to the kitchen ceiling in Spanish.

He was glad to have an errand. The house had filled with aunts who preempted every silence with questions about whether he was eating, and the questions were easier than the silence they replaced. He took the bus to the flower district, where the sidewalk buckets outside the shops held roses the color of wine and lilies like white trumpets, and, at the last stall before the corner, a flood of orange marigolds so bright they seemed lit from inside.

"Cempasúchil," the cashier said, when he only pointed. She pulled a bundle out of the bucket and shook the water off the stems. "For the Day of the Dead. My mother says the color and the smell guide the souls home." She said it the way people say things they have said every year since childhood, not like a lesson, just like weather. He bought two bundles. On the bus he held them in his lap and the scent came up off them, sharp and dusty and sweet, nothing like the flowers at the funeral home, which had smelled like nothing at all.

His mother met him at the door, and she went still when she saw them. He explained, awkwardly, half of what the cashier had said, and his mother pressed her wrist against her mouth and then took the bundles and said, "She would have liked that," and went to the kitchen, and he understood that in this house, for a while, everything he did was going to land somewhere soft and leave a mark.

Lyla came over that evening with his chemistry notes, which he had left in her car four days ago, before any of it, when his grandmother was still eating soup in the armchair and complaining that hospital blankets were too hedonistic, too soft, a person could sink in and never climb out. Lyla had never been to his house when it was full of aunts. She stood in the hallway holding the notebook against her chest like a shield, and she asked him if he wanted the notes for Monday, and he said probably there would be a test, and neither of them mentioned that the test was the least important thing either of them had thought about that day.

From where Lyla stood, she could see past him into the dining room, where the sideboard had become a small crowded country: photographs, a blue glass candleholder, the marigolds in a jar of water, their heads nodding. She had known his grandmother only as a voice through the screen door, calling Daniel inside in the summer. She watched him glance at the altar and then away, and she understood that he was not sad exactly, or not only sad, but occupied, the way a person is occupied carrying something heavy and level through a crowded room, unable to put it down and unable to gesture.

"Your grandmother was Mexican," she said. It came out as a question even though she already knew.

"Half of her was," Daniel said. "The half that mattered to flowers." He almost apologized for the sentence, because it sounded like something from a poem, and he did not want to be a person performing grief. But Lyla nodded like it had been useful, and she set the notebook on the hall table and took off her jacket, which was her way of saying she was staying.

Later, in the kitchen, he told her what he had worked out on the bus, that he had spent the week trying to decide whether his grandmother was gone or whether she was somewhere the way a place is somewhere, and he had hated both answers, because the first was unbearable and the second seemed like a lie he was telling himself. The marigolds had unsettled that. He did not believe, exactly, that a scent could guide anyone home. But somebody's mother had said it every autumn for a hundred years, and his grandmother had grown up inside that saying, and so the flowers were true even if they were not, and he could not make the two ideas lie down together, and he had stopped, on the bus, needing them to. He told Lyla he did not know what he believed and that this was the first honest sentence he had said all week. She said, "Okay," and got down two glasses, and on the sideboard in the dining room the orange heads were still open, facing the photographs, and his mother came in from the living room and began, without asking anyone, to cut bread.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Sugar bloom is a dry, gritty white coating caused when moisture dissolves sugar on the chocolate's surface and the sugar recrystallizes as it dries.
story:
The kitchen at Kobe's house smelled like cocoa butter and burnt sugar at the same time, which Morgan decided was the smell of ambition. Kobe's grandmother had left the double boiler out on the counter before her shift, along with three bars of dark chocolate and a note that said only, "Stir. Do not rush." Morgan had come over because she wanted, for once, to make something that turned out the way it was supposed to. Her school year had been a procession of almosts: an essay that missed the finalist round by one point, a chemistry lab that failed on the last step. Chocolate seemed mercifully simple. Melt it, cool it, pour it.

"Simple," Kobe said, leaning against the fridge and eating the evidence, which was a shard of last week's failed batch, gray and matte where it should have gleamed. "You keep saying that word."

"Simple compared to my life."

"Nothing about your life is simple. You changed your college essay topic four times."

"That's called revising," Morgan said, and dipped the spatula into the bowl.

The tempering itself was a kind of faith. She melted two thirds of the chocolate to a warmth she could barely hold her finger against, then chopped the remaining third fine and beat it in, watching the thermometer slide down degree by degree. Kobe read the numbers out loud like a countdown. The science, as far as Morgan could tell, was a matter of convincing the fat crystals to organize themselves into their most orderly form, the one that set with a shine and snapped instead of bending. She was trying to internalize the temperature sequence not as numbers on a card but as a feeling in her wrist, the way Kobe's grandmother clearly knew it, in the wrist and not the head.

They poured the first batch into molds and, because it was July and the kitchen was warm and Morgan was impatient, she slid the tray into the refrigerator. "It'll set faster," she said. Kobe shrugged and went to find the second bar.

Twenty minutes later the chocolates were firm, and wrong. A dry, gritty white coating lay across the top of every piece, powdery under her fingertip, like frost that had decided to become sand. Morgan stood at the open fridge door holding one up to the window light. It had not melted in transit. Nothing had melted. The chocolate underneath still snapped when she broke a corner off, cleanly even, but the surface was ruined, matte and rough where she had imagined a mirror.

She texted a photo to Quinn, who worked at the candy shop downtown and had opinions about everything. The reply came in three parts. "sugar bloom." Then: "happens when moisture gets at the sugar on the surface. the sugar dissolves, then recrystallizes as it dries, and that's your white coating." Then: "did you fridge them and take them out into a humid kitchen? because that's the classic move." Morgan looked at the window, where the July air pressed in, heavy with the day's rain. The chocolates had gone from cold fridge to humid room, and the room had done this to them. She set the flawed piece on the counter and got out her phone again, then put it down. She wanted to work the rest out herself.

The second batch she left on the marble counter Kobe's grandmother kept for pastry, in the coolest corner of the kitchen, out of the sun. They waited without saying much. Kobe washed the molds, and Morgan stirred the bowl slowly, watching the chocolate thicken to the texture of thick cream, and thought about her grandmother's ring, the one her mother kept in a drawer and called her patrimony, which Morgan had always found a strange word for something so small and so fought over. The ring was like the temper, maybe, or unlike it. She couldn't decide. Both were inherited techniques for making a thing hold its shape, and both seemed to require a patience nobody in the family had actually possessed.

"It's setting," Kobe said, crouched at counter level, chin on his folded arms, watching the molds like a person watching a fire. "Look at it. It's going shiny from the edges in."

It was. The shine crept across the surface the way the dark comes in at dusk, quietly and from the borders, until the whole top of each chocolate held the window light in one smooth plane. Morgan touched the edge of a piece, still faintly warm, and thought that the answer to the fridge had been to refuse the shortcut entirely. She also thought she would probably still use the fridge again someday, in a different kitchen, in a different summer, and that she could not promise herself otherwise. She tapped one chocolate out of its mold, broke it, and the snap was so sharp and clean that Kobe looked up.

"Okay," he said. "Do that again."

Morgan broke a second piece, and a third, lining them up along the counter's edge like evidence.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: In mayonnaise, lecithin and proteins from egg yolk act as emulsifiers, holding tiny oil droplets suspended in water so the sauce does not separate.
story:
Sebastian had promised the family a real dinner, cooked entirely by him, and he had chosen ambitious: roast chicken, green beans, and a garlic aioli he'd make from scratch. He was at the farmers' market on Saturday morning with his grandfather, who insisted on carrying the basket even though his hands had begun to shake a little, and who stopped at every stall as though each one required a diplomatic visit.

"You could just buy a jar of mayonnaise," his grandfather said, holding up a quart of eggs. "Nobody would know."

"I'd know."

"Ah." His grandfather set the eggs in the basket with great care. "That is the worst kind of knowing."

They found Wassim at his family's stall, weighing tomatoes for a line of customers, shouting prices with the confidence of someone auctioning cattle. When the line thinned he leaned over the display and grinned at Sebastian. "You're the aioli guy. Roland told me you're making some fancy dinner. He wants an invitation, by the way. He asked me to ask you, which is cowardly."

"Tell him if he brings dessert." Sebastian picked up a head of garlic, turned it over, put it back, picked it up again. The garlic was local, their county's own variety, autochthonous to these hills according to a hand-lettered sign, which Wassim had written mostly to annoy a rival vendor who imported everything. "Wassim, have you ever made mayonnaise?"

"My mom makes it when the good eggs come in. She says you have to respect the yolk. That's all the wisdom I have."

Sebastian nodded slowly, as though this were profound. In truth he was nervous, and the nervousness had a specific shape: he had read four recipes the night before and they disagreed. Some said add the oil in a thin stream. Some said drop by drop. One said a blender ruined the subtlety of the texture, hand-whisking was the only way, and another said hand-whisking was a myth invented to make people feel heroic. He wanted the dinner to be a kind of argument settled, his grandmother's old cooking and the recipes on his phone, both traditions brought to the table at once. He wasn't sure yet whether that was possible or whether he was just historicizing a sandwich spread, dressing up a condiment as a family project.

At home that evening he set up the kitchen while his parents were out. He separated the eggs, crushed the garlic with the flat of a knife the way his grandfather had shown him, and began to whisk. Yolk, garlic, mustard, a squeeze of lemon. Then the oil, drop by drop, his arm already aching. The mixture thickened, turned pale and glossy, and he felt a hot flare of pride, and then, somewhere between confident and halfway done, he poured the oil a little faster.

It broke. He watched it happen with a kind of clinical horror: the sauce thinned, went shiny and ragged, and then separated entirely, a pool of oil sitting on top of watery liquid like something that had given up. He stood over the bowl, whisk in hand, and considered, honestly, crying.

He called his grandfather instead.

"Describe it to me," his grandfather said, phone crackling.

"The oil's just sitting there. In liquid. It won't come back."

"It separated. Happened to me at your age, in your great-grandmother's kitchen, and she laughed at me for a week." A pause, the sound of a chair. "You still have yolks?"

"Two."

"Put a fresh yolk in a clean bowl. Whisk it a little. Then pour the broken mess in slowly, like it's the oil. Slowly, Sebastian. Slower than you think."

Sebastian cracked the new yolk into a clean bowl and beat it until it was smooth. Then, spoonful by spoonful, he whisked in the ruined sauce, and the impossible happened: it thickened, pulled together, turned silken and opaque, the oil folding back into the whole.

"It worked," he said into the phone. "Why did it work?"

"The lecithin and the proteins in the yolk," his grandfather said. "Emulsifiers. They hold the tiny oil droplets suspended in the water so the sauce doesn't separate. One yolk wasn't enough for how fast you poured. Two, apparently, were."

Sebastian looked at the bowl, at the sauce that had failed and then held. He still didn't know if the roast would be dry, or if Roland would actually show up with dessert or with Roland's usual contribution, which was an appetite. But he had a bowl of aioli that had come back from the dead, and dinner was two hours away, and the chicken went into the oven at five.

He set the timer and, because his arm deserved it, ate a spoonful standing up.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: The STAR method structures an interview answer as Situation, Task, Action and Result, so a story about past experience ends with what actually happened.
story:
Lauren had an interview on Saturday, ten o'clock, at the bakery on Fenwick Street, and she had told exactly one person about it, which was a mistake, because that person was Carlos. Carlos believed that information, once released, belonged to everybody, so by the end of warm-up laps half the team knew, and by the time they were stretching in a ring on the far field, Zakariya was waving his phone at her from across the circle.

"You're going to ramble," he said. "You always ramble when it matters."

"I do not."

"Tell the coach why you missed the car wash fundraiser. You gave her, like, nine sentences and the point was in none of them."

The coach blew the whistle for water, and Lauren dropped onto the grass beside Zakariya's bag while the others lined up at the cooler. She had practiced her answers in the mirror twice and hated both performances, the girl in the glass widening her eyes at herself like a stranger trying to seem friendly. "I don't know what to say when they ask about experience," she admitted. "I have experience. It just comes out sideways."

Zakariya turned his phone toward her. He was the sort of person who had a word-of-the-day app and used the words in sentences until they stopped being his and started being the team's, so nobody flinched anymore when he described the scrimmage as solipsism, eleven players all convinced they alone had the ball. He read aloud from the screen. "It's called the STAR method." Then he tapped through it with his thumb. "Situation, Task, Action, Result. So every answer is a story about something you actually did, and it ends with what actually happened. The ending is the part you always leave off."

"That's it?"

"That's it. Try one. Why do you want this job."

Lauren looked at the far goal, where the keeper was rolling balls back to the shooters. "Last summer my aunt's shop was short-staffed and I covered the register for three weeks. My job was the morning shift alone. I learned the register in two days and set up a clipboard so we'd stop running out of bags. We stopped running out of bags." She paused. "That felt like a person talking."

"It felt like a person who gets hired," Carlos said, arriving with a dripping water bottle and no shame about eavesdropping. "Now do eye contact. Do it on me." He sat cross-legged in front of her and stared with exaggerated intensity, unblinking, until she laughed. "No, seriously. Ms. Somsak says the same thing about defending. You watch the hips, not the ball. Watch their hips."

"That's the weirdest sentence you've ever said."

"Watch their hips, the interview version is, like, watch their eyes and not your shoes."

Ms. Somsak called them into a possession drill before Lauren could answer, and for forty minutes she thought about nothing but angles and pressure, which was the only reliable cure for thinking. But near the end, waiting on the touchline as a sub, she found the coach standing beside her, arms folded, watching the flow of play.

"Fenwick Street bakery," Ms. Somsak said, without looking over. "Saturday morning. You'll be fine if you answer the question they asked instead of six other ones." Then she sent Lauren on with a tap on the shoulder, and the game swallowed her again.

Afterward, in the parking lot, while her cleats dripped mud onto the asphalt and Carlos argued with Zakariya about whether the drill had been designed to expropriate their entire evening or merely most of it, Lauren ran the bakery answer once more under her breath. Situation, task, action, result. She could feel how the structure held the story steady, like a hand under a plate, and she could also feel what it cost, the way her aunt's hot cluttered shop came out of her mouth sanded down into four tidy rooms. There were true things the method left no space for: the smell of cardamom, the customer who called her "the boss" as a joke until it wasn't one. She would give them the clean version on Saturday. Whether that version would still be hers, afterward, was the question she carried to the car, key already out of her sock, unlocking the door in the dark.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
knowledge_domain: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
fact: A naive narrator, such as Huck in Mark Twain's Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, reports events honestly but misunderstands them, so readers see more than the narrator does.
story:
The bus smelled of rain and vinyl, and Amy had the window seat with the book balanced on her knee, the same water-stained paperback she'd been carrying since Monday. Tala dropped into the seat across the aisle, and Alannah followed, shaking water off her hood onto Amy's notes.

"You've read it three times now," Tala said, nodding at the cover. "It's not that long."

"That's the problem," Amy said. "Every time I read it, it's funnier, and I can't figure out why." She flipped to a page she'd marked with a gum wrapper. "This part. Huck goes to the Phelps farm pretending to be Tom Sawyer, and then the real Tom Sawyer shows up and pretends to be Huck. And Huck just reports it. He says he nearly fell over when Tom didn't blink. He doesn't get that Tom is delighted, that Tom's playing the game for the fun of it. Huck thinks he's watching a miracle."

Alannah leaned over the aisle, her elbow on Amy's seat. "So?"

"So it's funny because he doesn't get the joke. We get it. He doesn't. That's the whole engine." Amy tapped the gum wrapper. "And I've been writing my essay about how Twain uses humour, which is wrong, or half wrong, because the humour isn't Twain telling jokes. It's the gap. Huck says exactly what happened, and he's honest about all of it, and he still misses the meaning. That's why I trust him and don't trust him at the same time."

Mr. Dang, riding up front with his coffee because the boiler at the pool had flooded the equipment room again, turned around at the stoplight. "That's the paper on Huckleberry Finn? The one you stayed after class arguing about?"

"I wasn't arguing," Amy said. "I was asking a question."

"You were arguing," Tala said.

"I was asking why we call him unreliable when he never lies." The bus lurched over the tracks by the church, and Amy held the book flat with her palm. "He reports everything honestly. He tells us what he did and what he thought, even when it makes him look bad. But he misunderstands almost everything he sees. So the reader is always one step ahead, seeing more than he does, and he's the one telling the story." She looked up. "That's not lying. That's something else."

Mr. Dang sipped his coffee and said nothing, which was his way of making her keep going, and she knew it, and she kept going anyway.

"It's like the feud chapters," Alannah said, surprisingly, because Alannah had skimmed the book in one night and sworn off it. "The Grangerfords. Huck describes the house, the parlor, the crockery fruit, all the dead people in the drawings, and he admires it. He thinks it's grand. And you're reading it going, this family is going to kill each other over nothing, and he's standing there complimenting the wallpaper."

"The quagmire of it," Amy said, writing fast now on the back of her hand because the notes were in her bag under Alannah's wet hood. "Because he's honest, you believe every detail, so you build the whole picture out of true parts, and the picture he'd build out of the same parts is different. He'd say the feud was noble. You'd say it was insane. Same facts." The pen stalled. "But here's what I can't decide. Is Twain tricking us, or is he trusting us? Because if the reader has to do the work, then the reader who doesn't do it reads a whole different book. My little brother read it last year and just thought it was a raft book with a bad ending."

Tala laughed. "It is a raft book with a bad ending."

"It's not," Amy said, and then, more slowly, "or it is, if you read it flat. That's what I mean. The whole thing depends on where you're standing." Outside, the fields had gone to stubble, and the driver took the long corner past the grain elevator the way she always did, wide and unhurried. Amy watched the elevator slide across the glass and thought about her essay's first paragraph, which she'd written like a wound she was trying to cauterize with a thesis statement, one clean line to seal off the mess. It hadn't worked. The mess was the point.

She uncapped the pen again. "Naive narrator," she said, mostly to herself. "There's a name for it. I found it last night in the chapter on point of view. Huck is a naive narrator. That's the term."

"So use that," Alannah said.

"It's not that simple, because naive isn't the same as stupid, and I keep wanting to say it is, and then I read the part where he decides he'll go to hell rather than turn Jim in, and he means it, he genuinely thinks he's damned, and it's the most moral thing anyone in the book does. So he's naive and he's the best person in it. And the Widow Douglas and Miss Watson, who have all the education and the religion, are worse." She closed the book on her thumb. "So maybe the essay isn't about whether we trust him. Maybe it's about how. We trust his reporting and we discount his conclusions, and we have to do both at once, and the book makes us hold those apart for three hundred pages."

The bus hissed to its second stop and nobody got on. Rain ticked against the glass in the quiet.

"That's a real essay," Tala said. "That's actually a real essay."

"I don't know if I can write it," Amy said. "I don't know how to say both things without making it sound like one thing." She looked down at the back of her hand, where the ink had already smudged, the words going soft and blue across her knuckles. Mr. Dang raised his cup an inch, a toast or a dare, and turned back around as the driver pulled out onto the last stretch of road.

"Read me the opening line," Alannah said. "The one Twain put in the front."

"You know it."

"I want to hear you say it."
